A gap is an empty space, an opening, or a missing piece that exists between two things — where there should be something, but there isn't.

The key insight: a gap is almost always about separation. Two things exist, but there's a distance, a break, or a difference between them. That "in-between" is the gap.

1. A Physical Gap — a literal opening or space

This is the most concrete sense. When something that is normally closed, solid, or continuous has an opening or a break in it, that opening is a gap.

  • There's a gap in the fence where the dog slips through.
  • She smiled, and you could see a gap between her front teeth.
  • The hikers passed through a narrow gap in the mountains.
  • He peeked through a gap in the curtains.

The physical gap is essentially a hole or a space you can often see, walk through, or point to.

2. A Gap in Time — a stretch of time where something is missing or inactive

When there's a period of time between two events, or a period when something stopped happening, that pause is a gap.

  • After finishing school, she took a gap year to travel before starting university.
  • There was a ten-year gap between his first and second novel.
  • His résumé had a two-year gap — he had no job during that period.
  • The conversation had long, awkward gaps of silence.

Notice: the gap is the interval itself, the period in the middle where activity was absent.

3. An Abstract Gap — a difference, disparity, or missing connection between two things

This is the most widely used sense in modern language. When two things — ideas, groups, values, people — are further apart than they should be, or when something is missing that would bring them closer or complete the picture, that distance or absence is a gap.

  • There is a large gap between what he promises and what he delivers. (difference between words and actions)
  • The wealth gap between the rich and the poor has grown over the decades. (economic disparity)
  • She identified a gap in the market — nobody was selling affordable, stylish rain gear for children. (a missing product/opportunity)
  • The teacher noticed a gap in the student's knowledge of fractions. (a missing piece of understanding)
  • There is still a significant gender pay gap in many industries. (women earning less than men for equivalent work)
  • The book has a gap in its argument — it never explains why the policy failed. (a missing logical step)

In almost every use, a gap exists between two reference points. You can't have a gap in isolation — you need two sides:

  • A gap between two buildings
  • A gap between expectation and reality
  • A gap between generations
  • A gap between scientific research and public understanding

When someone says "bridge the gap" or "close the gap," they mean to reduce that distance, bring the two sides closer, or fill in what's missing.

Generation gap — the difference in values, attitudes, and communication styles between older and younger people. They often misunderstand each other because they grew up in very different worlds.

Gap year — a year taken off from formal education or work, usually to travel, volunteer, or explore. Common after high school or university.

Knowledge gap — a specific area of understanding that someone is missing.

Trade gap — when a country imports more goods than it exports; the shortfall between the two figures.

Credibility gap — the distance between what someone claims and what people believe to be true about them.

Mind the gap — a famous safety warning used on the London Underground (subway), asking passengers to be careful of the space between the train door and the platform edge. It's now used figuratively too, meaning "be aware of the difference between two things."

Fill/bridge/close/narrow the gap — all mean to reduce or eliminate the gap, to bring two things closer together or complete what's missing.

A gap implies incompleteness. When you say there's a gap in something, you're often hinting that it should be filled, corrected, or addressed. A gap in your skills means you need to learn something. A gap in an argument means it's weak. A gap in the market is an opportunity.

Gaps can be small or large. A tiny gap between tiles on a floor, or a massive gap in income between two countries — the word works at every scale.

Gaps can be neutral, negative, or even positive. A gap year is often seen as a positive thing. A wealth gap is seen as negative. A gap in a mountain range (like a mountain pass) is just neutral geography. Context tells you the tone.

"Gap" vs. "difference" — these overlap, but "gap" tends to feel more visual and spatial, even when used abstractly. A gap between two groups suggests they are standing apart, separated. A difference is more neutral — just a fact of being unlike. "Gap" often carries a slight sense that the separation is a problem or at least something noticeable.

Think of the word "gap" in any of its uses and you will almost always find the same underlying structure:

Two things exist. Something is missing between them. That missing thing — the space, the break, the absence, the distance — is the gap.

Whether it's a literal hole in a wall, a missing year on someone's CV, or the difference between how two social groups experience life — the word "gap" captures that sense of a space that separates, or a piece that's absent.
